newsitem.title: UK: Merger turns jet market into transatlantic duel.
newsitem.headline: Merger turns jet market into transatlantic duel.

text.p: Grudging approval of the merger between U.S. firms Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp (MDC) by the EU Commission, formally granted on Wednesday, turns the jet airliner industry effectively into a transatlantic duel.
Europe's Airbus Industrie was created in 1970 in a Franco-German effort to challenge the might of the U.S. civil aircraft industry in developing the next generation of airliners.
Now the four-nation consortium, which comprises British Aerospace Plc, France's Aerospatiale, the aerospace unit of Daimler-Benz AG and CASA of Spain, is Boeing's only big rival.
First Lockheed and then MDC dropped out of the race to develop new aircraft and concentrated their resources instead on their defence and space businesses.

Boeing reported orders for a record 717 jets valued at $53 billion last year but it had net orders for 559 airplanes with a list price value of $42.8 billion after excluding cancellations and conversions.
That compared with 301 jets worth about $21.6 billion for Airbus Industrie, while MDC took net orders for 38 jets valued at $2.2 billion.

Industry analysts have predicted that only MDC's new MD-95 twin-jet carrying 100 passengers and a freighter version of the MD-11 long-range tri-jet have any chance of future production under Boeing's ownership.

Older McDonnell Douglas DC-10 trijets, DC-9 and MD-80 twinjets are still a familiar sight at airports round the world, but the firm lost new sales in recent years as it failed to keep up with the increasing demand by big airlines for a greater choice of capacity and range configurations for their fleets.

Mindful that airlines prefer to source from a single manufacturer to rationalise their fleet operating costs, Airbus in contrast has been working hard to expand its own product range, which currently offers aircraft of 120-350 seats.

According to industry figures MDC aircraft account for nearly 25 percent of all airliners of over 100 seats in service round the world, but that figure is set to fall rapidly as new sales replace existing aircraft.
Boeing sales in recent years have averaged around 60 percent of the market for new airliners with Airbus holding 30 percent and MDC in third place with under six percent.
Airbus says it aims to increase its market share to 50 percent as it develops new aircraft to fill in the gaps at the top and bottom of its product range.

But looked at another way, Airbus member firms have also been saying they fear Airbus could lose market share if it does not fill those gaps soon. It must also restructure its cumbersome cooperative structure if it is to compete more effectively on cost and afford the new investment needed.

In particular Airbus is anxious to break Boeing's monopoly of the 747-400 'jumbo jet' market for aircraft with capacity for over 400 passengers as soon as possible because it says it is losing out on sales of smaller aircraft when an airline wants fleet commonality.

Airbus says it wants to get an all-new 500 to 550-seat doubledecker aircraft, the A3XX, into the air by the year 2003 for roughly the same price as a planned stretch version of the 747-400, at around $200 million.
But it needs to fund development costs currently estimated at over $8.0 billion and is therefore seeking outside investors.

To help close the gap from below, Airbus also launched plans at the Paris air show in June to offer new derivatives of its 340 four-engine long range jet which will take capacity up to 378 seats, from around 260-300 seats on the existing versions, depending on range.
But for the time being Boeing still offers the widest range of aircraft. The following is a summary of aircraft currently produced by all three manufacturers:
BOEING CO
B737. Narrow-body, twin-engine jet is world's biggest selling airliner, with more than 2,900 delivered into service. Range about 2,500 miles in current version.
New generation 737-600, -700 and -800 versions scheduled to enter commercial service in October and will seat from 108-189 in mixed-class configuration.
B757. Twin-engine, narrow-body sister to 767, seats 194. First delivery 1982. Total in service 760 including freighters. Range 3,200 to 4,500 statute miles.
B767. Wide-body, twin-engine carries 218 in three classes. Entered service in 1982; total deliveries 663. Range 3,800 to 7,600 statute miles, depending on version.

B777. Boeing's newest model, entered service in 1995 and is world's largest twin-engine jet. Seats 305 to 394 in three classes, range 4,300 to 8,200 statute miles, depending on version. Boeing has delivered 76 and has received orders for more than 300.

B747-400. Current version of world's largest commercial jet holds 400-425 in three-class configuration, depending on range. Powered by four engines and also available in freighter and combi versions. Range 8,290 statute miles with 1,100 delivered into service since initial delivery of 747-100 in 1970.
MCDONNELL DOUGLAS
MD-80. Twin-engine, narrow-body jet, seats 130-155 with range of 1,800 to 2,880 statute miles. About 1,150 delivered since entering service in 1980.

MD-90. Twin-engine, narrow body rated quietest large commercial jet in service. Seats 153 with range of 2,400 to 3,200 miles. Entered service 1995. Company has delivered 49 and has firm orders for 96 more.
MD-95. Smaller, twin-engine craft seats 106 with range of 1,781 miles. Programme launched in 1995 with order for 50 jets from ValuJet Inc but no other orders received. First delivery scheduled 1999.
MD-11. Widebody trijet. More than 160 in service since first delivery 1990. Seats 233 to 410, range 4,500 to 8,300 miles. Freighter version gaining popularity.
AIRBUS INDUSTRIE
A319. New version of A320 series narrowbody twinjets with 124 seats in two-class configuration and range of 3,500 to 6,500 kilometres, 32 in service and 115 more on order as at end of May.
A320. Twinjet, seats 150 in two-class configuration, range of 4,900-5,500 kilometres. 568 in service and 260 more on order at end of May.
A321. Stretch version of A320 seating 185 passengers in two-class with range of 4,250 to 5,500 kilometres. 70 aircraft delivered and 145 still on order.
A310-300 Veteran widebody twinjet seating 220 passengers in two-class with range of 8,000-9,600 kilometres. 254 aircraft produced with seven more still to be delivered.
A300-600R Widebody twinjet seating 266 passengers in two class with range of 7,500 kilometres. 462 aircraft delivered with 25 more still on order.
A330 Widebody twinjet seating up to 335 passengers in two classes with range of 8,900 kilometres. 58 aircraft delivered with 122 more on order.

A340-300 Current version of widebody four-engined aircraft capable of flying low density ultra long-haul routes. Seats 260 to 295 passengers in three-class configuration flying 12,000 to 13,300 kilometres. 110 aircraft delivered and further 71 on order.
